analysis.title: Wargaming The AI Crash: TS Lombard Sees A $20 Trillion Wipeout... But Only A "Mild" Recession
key_insights: TS Lombard's Dario Perkins assumes the AI capex boom ends and models the fallout. Scenario: S&P 500 down 30%, tech down 40%, other sectors down 20%, about $20 trillion of market cap lost, credit losses on AI-related debt of $125-190 billion.

Perkins expects only a mild US recession, comparable to 1990 or 2001 and not the GFC. His reasons: private-sector balance sheets are healthy, policy room is large, and rate cuts would work because the bottom of the 'K' (housing, durables, low-end consumption) has pent-up demand.

He does not pick a trigger and calls the crash 'overdetermined'. He names six vulnerabilities: revenue disappointment, emerging credit risks, the 'teaser rate' problem, upcoming IPOs, the semiconductor cycle, and regulatory and safety backlash.

Revenue: US tech spends about $1 trillion a year on the AI buildout. Studies put the revenue needed to justify it at $2.5-3.0 trillion by 2030, about 14 times today's figure. Perkins' ratio of 'internal' to 'external' ecosystem revenue is little changed since June, so the boom is still capex recycling and circular financing.

80% of OpenAI and Anthropic revenue comes from 1% of customers, mostly VC-funded startups. Ramp data showed two months of almost no growth in token spend. Chinese open-weight models now carry more than half the tokens on Vercel's gateway ('China shock 3.0').

Credit: debt is the marginal source of AI funding, with about $700 billion of AI bonds expected in 2027. Hidden liabilities such as Meta's Hyperion/Beignet lease structure are estimated at $1.5-2 trillion by Perkins. Post-GFC research says the pace of borrowing, not the level of debt, predicts crises, and the pace is accelerating.

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave already pay about 15% on debt. ZeroHedge adds that CoreWeave's 2032 bonds fell below 80 cents with yields near 16%, and that CDS priced roughly 63% odds of default last week.

'Teaser rate' problem: depreciation only starts once data centers enter service, and lab lease commitments only start once capacity is running. Seller backlog grows while buyer expense is deferred. AI finances could look very different in 12 months. Morgan Stanley sees hyperscaler and neocloud free cash flow at its most negative in late 2027, with cash burn near $600 billion including leases.

IPOs: the Dotcom top coincided with lockup expiries. OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs would force disclosure on 'annual recurring revenue' metrics that Perkins says are designed to flatter. CoreWeave founders sold $3.3 billion before the selloff.

Semiconductor cycle: over 55% of incoming investment in AI firms comes from other AI firms (BIS), vendor-financing deals have risen sharply, and double and triple ordering risks turning today's shortage into a glut.
Regulatory backlash: about 55% of Americans want AI development slowed and 13% do not. One serious AI-assisted cyberattack could produce a less tech-friendly Washington after the midterms.

Core mechanism: AI capex need only slow its growth to cause a crash. Frontier labs with no profits are likened to NINJA subprime borrowers, with the data center as collateral and contracted payments as debt service. The structure holds only while the lab can keep raising money.

Equity exposure: tech is a record 40%+ of the US market and semis nearly 20%. Bulls cite a trailing tech P/E near 30 against 70-75 in the Dotcom era. Perkins counters that earnings are recycled capex and hyperscaler 'other' revenue is mostly valuation gains on stakes in other AI companies.

Credit losses: total AI-related debt is about $2.9 trillion, with almost 25% assumed vulnerable. A 35% cumulative default rate over 2028-30 and 25-50% recovery gives $125-190 billion of losses. Perkins calls this material but not systemic. Hyperscalers are seen as sound credits, with the stress in neoclouds, single-asset vehicles, Oracle, OpenAI, Anthropic and app startups.

Upstream borrowers will owe about $545 billion in bonds, $920 billion in bank loans and $650 billion in private credit by end-2027. Perkins' analogy is the late-1980s S&L crisis. ZeroHedge notes that seven of 20 junk-rated AI data center bonds rely on a single tenant.

Real economy: data center capex is import-intensive, so a collapse cuts imports and offsets much of the GDP hit. Net US GDP level falls about 2%pt, in line with the IMF's latest WEO, as tech capex round-trips from near 5% of GDP in 2027.

Labor: data center construction has created about 500K jobs, possibly 800K by end-2027. Losing them adds about 50bps to unemployment. Perkins argues the wealth effect on spending is weak since the link between net worth and the savings rate broke after 2016. ZeroHedge notes the top 10% account for about half of US consumer spending.

Fed context: the real policy rate is near 2%, giving room to cut. ZeroHedge says the Fed under Kevin Warsh has been hiking into 3.7% CPI and 5%+ 10Y yields and only paused last week because credit tightened for it. Oil near $100 and a diesel squeeze into 2027 could limit easing.

Positioning, bonds: Perkins argues an AI crash is a demand shock, so yields fall. This conflicts with colleague Steven Blitz, who three weeks ago argued the 10Y is headed to 8%. Last week yields fell even as CPI and PPI ran hot.
Positioning, equities: favor non-US stocks. Korea and Taiwan would be hit hard (Taiwan tech exports about 40% of GDP), while Europe and the rest should outperform.
Positioning, dollar: Perkins expects the crash to be dollar-negative, with flows to the euro, yen and possibly sterling. After Dotcom the dollar was flat for 18 months and then fell.

Timing: TS Lombard assumes the capex boom ends in early 2028, though the date could slip. Going short US tech or long duration too early is a career risk. Recommendation (from GMO's Ben Inker): treat AI as an 'easy' bubble, hold normal risk in diversified global stocks, and add duration as AI strains emerge.

Perkins' downside risk: an AI crash could trigger AI-driven layoffs that did not appear during the boom, giving a slow, jobless recovery. He also expects Fed easing could inflate a new residential property bubble, as after Dotcom.

ZeroHedge dissent: strains Perkins wants to see before adding duration already appeared in credit last week. Meta raised capex guidance, joined Amazon in negative free cash flow, added $76 billion of off-balance sheet commitments and fell 6% at the open, erasing $100 billion. ZeroHedge expects credit to force the issue before 2028.

tension_points.bull_case: TS Lombard expects only a mild US recession like 1990 or 2001. Balance sheets are healthy, there is policy room, and rate cuts revive the bottom of the 'K'. Credit losses of $125-190 billion are not systemic.
tension_points.bear_case: ZeroHedge argues credit stress will force the issue before 2028 and that 'contained' is doing a lot of work, since seven of 20 junk-rated AI data center bonds depend on a single tenant. Inflation at 3.7% and oil near $100 may keep the Fed from easing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The Fed fails to pivot from hiking to cutting fast enough, inflation does not behave, or losses spread beyond the neoclouds.

tension_points.bull_case: Perkins: an AI crash is a demand shock and yields fall, as in every recession except the 1970s. Last week yields fell even as CPI and PPI ran hot.
tension_points.bear_case: Steven Blitz argued three weeks ago that the 10Y is headed to 8% on fiscal dominance.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Yields rising in the face of AI credit stress would undercut the demand-shock view.

tension_points.bull_case: TS Lombard assumes capex ends in early 2028, leaving time to hold normal risk and add duration later.
tension_points.bear_case: ZeroHedge says AI strains already showed up in credit last week and Meta's capex raise makes the 'second derivative' problem a near-term issue.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further credit stress or capex guidance cuts before 2028 would show the timing is too late.
